_comment: Ascites is a SHORT CASE: differential diagnosis of free peritoneal fluid, examined as its own syndrome rather than assumed to be the chronic-liver-disease long case. Same shape as anaemia.json: chapters lean on shared skills, minimal new local skills, differential IS the core content.
name: Ascites
oneLine: Free fluid in the peritoneum, and the four categories that put it there

chapters.blurb: Identical to any other short case

chapters.title: General examination
chapters.blurb: The JVP and the stigmata, not just the belly

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Look for stigmata of chronic liver disease, facial puffiness of a nephrotic pattern, and cachexia, each pointing towards a different one of the four categories before you have percussed a single flank.

skill.gen.edema.expect: Note whether the oedema is dependent and pitting (cardiac, hepatic, renal) or periorbital and generalised (more typical of a nephrotic pattern), and whether it appeared before or after the abdominal swelling.

chapters.title: Putting the picture together
chapters.blurb: Ascites plus the one other finding that names the cause

skill.exam.gi.ascites.expect: Grade the ascites (mild/moderate/large) and specifically check for tenderness or fever alongside it, which should raise spontaneous bacterial peritonitis if a hepatic cause is already suspected.

skill.exam.gi.liver.expect: A firm, irregular, shrunken liver supports a hepatic cause; a smooth, tender, enlarged liver with a raised JVP supports a cardiac cause instead.

skill.exam.gi.spleen.expect: Splenomegaly alongside ascites supports a portal hypertensive, usually hepatic, cause.

stations.title: Assess this patient's ascites and give your differential
stations.task: This patient has noticed abdominal swelling for three weeks. Examine for ascites and its likely cause, and present your findings with a differential in six minutes.
examinerQuestions: Roughly how much fluid is needed for the sign you elicited to become positive?
What single other examination finding would most help you decide between a cardiac and a hepatic cause?
If you tapped this ascites, what two values would you need to calculate a SAAG?

cases.title: A farmer whose belly has been swelling for three months
cases.opening: Narayan Reddy, 54, has come to the medical outpatient department with abdominal swelling. He is sitting with his hands resting on a visibly distended abdomen. Introduce yourself and take a history.
cases.fallback: I am not sure what you mean, doctor. Can you ask that a different way?

patient.name: Narayan Reddy
patient.occupation: Farmer, grows sugarcane on his own land
patient.residence: Rural, lives with his wife and two adult sons

presenting.reply: Doctor, my belly has been swelling for about three months. It has been getting bigger and bigger, and now my clothes do not fit. My legs have also started swelling in the last month.

onset_order.reply: The belly started first, doctor, well before the legs. The legs only started about four weeks ago.

rate.reply: It came on slowly, week by week. It was not sudden at all.

alcohol.reply: I drink country arrack most evenings, doctor. Maybe four to five drinks a day, for close to twenty-five years now. I have not touched it in the last two weeks because I have been unwell.

jaundice.reply: Yes, my wife told me my eyes looked a little yellow about two months ago. It has not gone away completely.

gi_bleed.reply: No, doctor, I have never vomited blood, and my stools have always looked normal.

sensorium.reply: My son says I have been more forgetful lately and sleep during the day, then stay awake most of the night. I had not noticed it myself.

orthopnea.reply: No, I sleep flat with one pillow and I do not wake up short of breath.

frothy_urine.reply: No, my urine looks normal, and my face has not been puffy in the mornings.

weight_appetite.reply: My appetite has been poor for the last two months, but I think most of the swelling is fluid, not weight loss.

fever_ts.reply: No fever, no night sweats. Nobody at home has tuberculosis that I know of.

abdominal_pain.reply: It feels tight and heavy, but there is no real pain, and no fever with it.

breathlessness.reply: Only when the belly is very full, then it is hard to take a deep breath. Otherwise I am fine walking around the farm.

leg_swelling.reply: Both my ankles are puffy by evening, worse than in the morning.

drug_history.reply: I started a water tablet from a local doctor about three weeks ago. I do not know the name. I also take a painkiller sometimes for my knees.

past_illness.reply: No diabetes, no blood pressure problem, no heart disease that I know of. No operations.

family.reply: No one in my family has had liver trouble that I know of.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Icteric sclera, mildly wasted with temporal hollowing, multiple spider naevi over the upper chest and neck, palmar erythema sparing the centre of the palms. JVP not raised. No gynaecomastia noted on brief inspection.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Pulse 88 regular. Blood pressure 108/68. Respiratory rate 18. Temperature 37.0 C. SpO2 98 percent on room air.

skill.gen.edema.finding: Bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin, equal on both sides, worse by evening. No calf tenderness.

skill.exam.gi.ascites.finding: Abdomen generally distended with flank fullness. Shifting dullness positive on both sides after adequate repositioning. Fluid thrill not tested given the volume is only moderate. Umbilicus everted but not weeping.

skill.exam.gi.gallbladder_kidney.finding: Gallbladder not palpable. Kidneys not ballotable bilaterally.

skill.exam.gi.liver.finding: Liver edge just palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin, firm, irregular margin, span reduced to 9 cm on percussion (upper border heavy, lower border light). Non-tender.

skill.exam.gi.spleen.finding: Spleen palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin on deep inspiration, firm, non-tender, moving with respiration, notch felt.

skill.exam.gi.ascites_cause.finding: JVP not raised, no parasternal heave, no third heart sound: no cardiac features. Stigmata of chronic liver disease present alongside a shrunken firm liver and a mildly enlarged spleen, in keeping with a portal hypertensive, hepatic cause. No doughy abdomen, no palpable lymphadenopathy.

ascitic_tap.label: Diagnostic ascitic tap with paired serum albumin
ascitic_tap.result: Ascitic albumin 0.9 g/dL against a serum albumin 2.5 g/dL, giving a SAAG of 1.6 g/dL. Neutrophil count 80 cells/mm3. Culture bottle inoculated at the bedside, pending.
ascitic_tap.note: This is the test that does most of the work in one sitting: SAAG 1.6 is high, predicting portal hypertension, and the neutrophil count is well below the 250/mm3 threshold, so spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is not present today.

lft.label: Liver function tests
lft.result: Bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL (mostly conjugated), AST 96, ALT 58, alkaline phosphatase mildly raised, albumin 2.5 g/dL.
lft.note: AST greater than ALT with a low albumin fits ongoing alcohol-related hepatocellular injury on a background of chronic disease, not an acute cholestatic process.

coag.label: Prothrombin time / INR
coag.note: Prolonged, reflecting reduced synthetic function, and needed before any planned tap or procedure.

cbc.label: Full blood count
cbc.result: Haemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, white cells 5.1 x10^9/L, platelets 88 x10^9/L.
cbc.note: Thrombocytopenia here fits hypersplenism from portal hypertension rather than marrow disease, given the splenomegaly already found on examination.

usg.label: Ultrasound abdomen with Doppler
usg.result: Coarse, nodular liver echotexture with a shrunken right lobe and enlarged caudate lobe. Splenomegaly, span 13 cm. Moderate ascites. Portal vein patent, diameter 14 mm, with reduced flow velocity.
usg.note: Confirms cirrhotic morphology and a patent, but dilated, portal vein, consistent with portal hypertension rather than thrombosis.

ca125.label: Serum CA-125
ca125.note: Not indicated as a diagnostic test here: CA-125 is nonspecifically raised by peritoneal irritation from ascites of almost any cause, cirrhosis included, and ordering it in a patient with obvious alcoholic cirrhosis and a high SAAG mainly generates an unnecessary ovarian-cancer workup.

ana.label: Antinuclear antibody
ana.note: No clinical feature here (young age, other autoimmune disease, an atypical pattern) suggested autoimmune hepatitis; sent as a reflex, not because a question was actually being asked.

ascitic_ada.label: Ascitic fluid adenosine deaminase
ascitic_ada.note: There is no fever, no night sweats and no weight loss out of proportion to the fluid itself, so tuberculous peritonitis was not the leading concern; sending ADA on every tap regardless of the clinical picture is exactly the reflex-panel habit this case is meant to discourage.

differentialModel.answer: Ascites due to decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis, high-SAAG and portal hypertensive. Consider cardiac ascites, nephrotic syndrome, and tuberculous or malignant peritonitis.

diagnosis.answer: Decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis with moderate-volume, high-SAAG ascites, no spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and early hepatic encephalopathy.

managementModel.answer: Sodium restriction and an aldosterone antagonist, adding a loop diuretic if the response is inadequate, with regular weight and renal function checks. Stop the unsupervised diuretic and the painkiller he has been taking. Treat the early encephalopathy, screen again for a GI bleed given the low platelets, and support alcohol cessation. Large-volume paracentesis with albumin replacement if the ascites becomes tense, and continued surveillance for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and for hepatocellular carcinoma.

teachingPoints: The order of swelling did real work before any examination: the abdomen distended weeks before the legs, which is the hepatic and malignant pattern, not the cardiac or renal one where legs usually lead.

His family noticing forgetfulness and a reversed sleep pattern, which he himself had not noticed, is grade 1 hepatic encephalopathy. It is only ever caught by asking a relative, never by asking the patient alone.
The liver is small and firm with a reduced span, not enlarged. A cirrhotic liver often shrinks as it scars, and mistaking 'no hepatomegaly' for 'no liver disease' is a common error.
Low platelets here are not an incidental finding: they reflect hypersplenism from portal hypertension and directly explain the palpable spleen found on the same examination.

An unsupervised diuretic and an NSAID-type painkiller, started weeks apart from anyone reviewing his renal function, are both plausible contributors to any deterioration and are worth stopping before adding more drugs.

The SAAG of 1.6 confirms what the stigmata already suggested: this is portal hypertensive ascites. The neutrophil count, not the appearance of the fluid, is what rules out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis today, not tomorrow.

CA-125 was sent and came back raised, but it says nothing here: it rises with peritoneal irritation from ascites of any cause, and ordering it in a patient with an already-explained SAAG only manufactures a false alarm.

skill.exam.gi.ascites_cause.title: Reading the cause from the rest of the examination
skill.exam.gi.ascites_cause.oneLine: Ascites plus one other finding usually names the category before any fluid is sent
skill.exam.gi.ascites_cause.why: The fluid itself looks the same in the flanks whatever the cause. What actually narrows the differential at the bedside is everything found ALONGSIDE the ascites: the JVP, the stigmata, the oedema pattern, and the consistency of any mass.
skill.exam.gi.ascites_cause.body: Examine ascites as part of a wider survey, deliberately looking for the finding that would confirm or refute each of the four broad categories.
pitfalls: Examining the ascites in isolation without checking the JVP, which is the single fastest way to catch a cardiac cause.
Assuming ascites with mild pedal oedema must be hepatic without looking for stigmata to actually support that.
Missing a doughy abdomen or lymphadenopathy that would point towards tuberculosis or malignancy.

probes.q: A patient with ascites has a raised JVP with a prominent wave and bibasal crackles. What cause does this point towards?
probes.a: A cardiac cause, such as right heart failure or constrictive pericarditis, rather than a primary hepatic one.

probes.q: Describe the classic abdominal palpation finding in tuberculous peritonitis.
probes.a: A 'doughy' abdomen: a diffuse, indistinct resistance to palpation, often with matted bowel loops or lymph nodes, rather than a discrete mass.

probes.q: Why does the absence of any stigmata of chronic liver disease, in a patient with new ascites and weight loss, change your leading differential?
probes.a: It argues against a hepatic cause and shifts the leading differential towards malignant or tuberculous peritoneal disease, or a renal cause, prompting a SAAG and cytology-directed rather than a purely hepatic workup.

keyPoints: Cardiac: raised JVP with a prominent wave, a displaced or abnormal apex, a third heart sound, bibasal crackles, and pitting oedema that is often as marked as the ascites itself.
Hepatic: stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia), splenomegaly from portal hypertension, and caput medusae with flow away from the umbilicus.
Renal/nephrotic: generalised oedema, notably periorbital and not just dependent, with relatively few stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Malignant/tuberculous: a hard, irregular, fixed abdominal or pelvic mass, matted lymphadenopathy, or a doughy, indistinctly resistant abdomen on palpation (the classic description in tuberculous peritonitis), often with cachexia.

A completely normal cardiac, hepatic and renal examination, with weight loss and low-grade fever, should raise tuberculous or malignant peritoneal disease even before any single confirmatory finding is present.

skill.ascites.differential.title: Differential diagnosis of ascites
skill.ascites.differential.oneLine: The serum-ascites albumin gradient is the modern discriminator, not transudate versus exudate
skill.ascites.differential.why: Ascites has a long list of causes, and memorising them unsorted is useless at the bedside. The serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) sorts almost all of them into two physiologically distinct groups and should organise how you think about every new case.
skill.ascites.differential.body: Calculate SAAG as serum albumin minus ascitic fluid albumin, and use it as the primary branch point in the differential.
pitfalls: Sending an ascitic tap without a paired serum albumin, so the SAAG cannot actually be calculated.
Using the old transudate/exudate cutoffs for ascitic fluid rather than SAAG.
Forgetting that a high SAAG does not mean 'hepatic'; heart failure and Budd-Chiari also produce a high SAAG.

probes.q: How is SAAG calculated, and what value predicts portal hypertension?
probes.a: Serum albumin minus ascitic fluid albumin; a gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more predicts portal hypertension with about 97 percent accuracy.

probes.q: Name three causes of a HIGH SAAG ascites.
probes.a: Cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, massive hepatic metastases, Budd-Chiari syndrome, portal vein thrombosis.

probes.q: A patient has ascites with a SAAG of 0.6 g/dL. What broad category of cause does this point to, and name two examples.
probes.a: A low-SAAG, non-portal-hypertensive cause: peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculous peritonitis, nephrotic syndrome, pancreatic or biliary ascites, or bowel obstruction/infarction.

probes.q: Why has SAAG replaced the transudate/exudate classification specifically for ascites?
probes.a: Because SAAG is a better physiological discriminant for the causes of ascites (reflecting whether portal hypertension is driving the fluid) than the older protein-based transudate/exudate split, which performs less reliably in this fluid compared with, for example, pleural fluid.

keyPoints: SAAG = serum albumin minus ascitic fluid albumin. A gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more predicts portal hypertension as the cause with about 97 percent accuracy.

High SAAG (1.1 g/dL or more, 'portal hypertensive'): cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, cardiac causes (heart failure, constrictive pericarditis), massive hepatic metastases, Budd-Chiari syndrome, portal vein thrombosis.
Low SAAG (under 1.1 g/dL): peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculous peritonitis, pancreatic ascites, biliary ascites, nephrotic syndrome, bowel obstruction or infarction, serositis.

SAAG has replaced the older transudate-versus-exudate classification for ascites specifically, because it is a better physiological discriminant; the transudate-exudate framework remains useful for pleural fluid but is not the modern approach here.
Ascites appearing BEFORE generalised oedema ('ascites praecox') is a specific pattern associated with chronic constrictive pericarditis.

Ascites without significant leg oedema at all suggests chronic constrictive pericarditis, tuberculous or malignant peritonitis, pancreatic ascites, or acute Budd-Chiari syndrome, each of which causes ascites by a mechanism that does not also raise systemic venous pressure or lower albumin enough to cause dependent oedema.

skill.ix.ascites.workup.title: Working up new ascites
skill.ix.ascites.workup.oneLine: A diagnostic tap answers most of the question in one sitting
skill.ix.ascites.workup.why: Nearly every new ascites should be tapped once, deliberately, sending the right panel the first time, because a repeat tap for a forgotten test costs the patient a second procedure.
skill.ix.ascites.workup.body: A diagnostic paracentesis, paired with a same-day serum sample, does most of the discriminating work in one step; imaging and further tests follow the SAAG result.
pitfalls: Tapping ascitic fluid without a same-day serum albumin, losing the SAAG.
Waiting for culture results before treating a neutrophil count of 250/mm3 or more.
Not inoculating culture bottles at the bedside, which significantly reduces the yield compared with sending fluid to the lab in a plain container.
Ordering a full malignancy and TB workup on every tap regardless of the SAAG and the clinical picture, rather than being directed by them.

probes.q: What test must be sent alongside the ascitic albumin to actually calculate SAAG?
What ascitic neutrophil count mandates immediate antibiotic treatment, without waiting for culture?
probes.a: 250 cells per cubic millimetre or more.

probes.q: Why should ascitic fluid be inoculated into blood culture bottles at the bedside rather than sent to the lab in a plain container?
probes.a: Bedside inoculation significantly improves the culture yield compared with sending fluid in a plain container, because it gets the fluid into an enriched medium immediately rather than after a delay.

keyPoints: Diagnostic paracentesis: cell count with differential, albumin (for SAAG, needs a paired serum albumin sent the same day), total protein, and culture in a blood culture bottle at the bedside for the best yield.
A neutrophil count of 250 cells/mm3 or more in ascitic fluid is the threshold used to diagnose spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and demands immediate antibiotic treatment, not a wait for culture.
If tuberculosis is suspected: send adenosine deaminase (ADA) and consider cytology and, where available, fluid for AFB and TB-PCR alongside imaging.
If malignancy is suspected: cytology on the tapped fluid, and imaging (ultrasound or CT) to look for a primary and for peritoneal deposits.
Ultrasound abdomen confirms the ascites, assesses liver echotexture and portal flow, screens for a mass, and can guide the tap in a difficult abdomen.

Directed blood work follows the leading category: liver function tests and coagulation for a hepatic cause, a full renal panel with urine protein for a renal cause, and an echocardiogram where a cardiac cause is suspected.

skill.dx.ascites.title: Stating the diagnosis of ascites
skill.dx.ascites.oneLine: Grade it, give the SAAG-based category, and name the leading cause
skill.dx.ascites.why: 'Ascites' alone is an observation. A complete statement grades how much fluid there is, states whether it is portal hypertensive or not, and commits to a leading cause.
skill.dx.ascites.body: State it in three parts: grade, SAAG category, and leading cause pending or supported by the workup.
pitfalls: Writing 'ascites' with no grade or SAAG category.
Naming a cause the SAAG result actually contradicts.
Omitting whether spontaneous bacterial peritonitis has been actively excluded when the cause is hepatic.

probes.q: Give the three parts of a complete ascites diagnostic statement.
probes.a: The grade, the SAAG category (high or low), and the leading cause.

probes.q: Why is 'ascites, likely hepatic' an incomplete statement even after a tap has been done?
probes.a: It omits the actual grade and the SAAG value that justifies calling it hepatic, and does not say whether spontaneous bacterial peritonitis has been looked for and excluded, all of which change immediate management.

keyPoints: Grade: mild (detectable only by ultrasound), moderate (moderate symmetrical distension), or large/gross (marked distension), following the International Ascites Club grading, or the older 1+ to 4+ traditional scale.
SAAG category: high (portal hypertensive) or low (non-portal-hypertensive), from the paired albumin measurement.
Leading cause, stated even when provisional: for example 'high-SAAG ascites, likely cirrhotic, pending confirmation of chronic liver disease' is a complete and honest statement.

Worked example: 'Large-volume ascites, SAAG 1.4 g/dL (high, portal hypertensive), most likely due to decompensated cirrhosis given the associated stigmata of chronic liver disease, with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis excluded on cell count.'
